name: E2E Shared Storage - One Granted Account, Two Devices Writing
description:
The acceptance test for account-keyed writer sets (#3344). A `SharedStorage` writer set names ACCOUNTS, so one grant must cover every device its holder owns — and a signature only ever names a KEY, so the receiver has to resolve that key to an account at the write's causal cut before it can match the set. Everything about that resolution is unit-tested; this is the only thing that proves it over the real wire, where the two nodes hold different amounts of the device-binding history.
Distinct from `account-device-revoke-lockout`, which proves the same one-account-two-devices story on the MEMBERSHIP plane with plain KV writes. Membership and writer sets are separate gates resolved by separate code: a paired device can be a perfectly good context member and still have every guarded write refused. That is precisely the bug this scenario would have caught — two account spaces, where a node's own writes were refused by every peer — so the planes need separate coverage.
What each phase is load-bearing for:

  1. Three nodes. node-1 is admin and the context creator, so it is the sole
     initial writer. node-2 is Alice's laptop, a namespace member. node-3 is
     Alice's phone: DELIBERATELY never invited, never granted, and never named
     in the writer set. One device per node, because `NodeDeviceIdentity` is
     keyed per namespace.

  2. node-1 grants Alice's ACCOUNT — one call, `shared_add_writer`. The
     account has to be read out of node-2 (`my_account`), because an account is
     derived from a node's root rather than carried on the wire, so a scenario
     has no other way to learn one.

  3. The laptop writes the shared value and node-1 reads it. Baseline: the
     grant works for the device that was present when it was made.

  4. The phone is paired onto Alice's account and writes the SAME shared
     value, with no second grant and no rotation. This is the feature. Two
     assertions carry it: the phone's `my_account` equals the laptop's — one
     principal, two devices — and the writer set is byte-identical before and
     after the phone's write, so nothing was added on its behalf.

     It is also the step that needs the receiver-side resolution: the phone's
     action is signed by a key that appears in no writer set anywhere. A
     receiver that resolved the signer from its own identity, or refused a key
     it could not name, would drop this write — and a receiver that accepted
     it unresolved would let any key claim any account.

  5. The authored plane, which is the same account gate over a different
     principal. The phone updates an entry the LAPTOP filed, with no grant of
     its own: an authored entry's owner is the account, so one person reaches
     their own note from either machine. The signature still names the phone's
     key, so this only passes if the receiver resolves that key to Alice's
     account — the same resolution step 4 needs, on a second plane.

     What stays per device is the per-writer state underneath: an LWW
     tiebreak, a counter slot, an HLC seed. Moving THOSE onto accounts is what
     makes two devices of one person clobber each other, and it is a different
     mistake from this one. Both compile — `AccountId` and `PublicKey` are
     both 32 bytes.

What this does NOT cover (intentionally):
  * A deferral: a receiver that has not yet folded the binding must retry
    rather than refuse. Real nodes here settle before every read, so the gap
    never opens. It is pinned in `calimero-storage`'s
    `deferred_signer_convergence` tests, which can hold two receivers at
    different fold depths on purpose.
  * Revocation of the paired device. That is `account-device-revoke-lockout`'s
    job, on the membership plane; the writer plane's half is unit-tested in
    `calimero-op-adapter`.

User-visible failure mode this guards against: "I was granted write access, and then my second device got permission denied."

Each of the original scenario's nodes is an account here; see merobox/cloud_v2/port.py for the mapping.
account_pair output credential (v1 device key) x1: checks what the dropped steps did
json_assert statement on a dropped step's output x1: checks what the dropped steps did
login (unknown) x3: checks what the dropped steps did
wait_for_sync x8: replication is synchronous: a read sees every committed write

steps.name: Install application on shared-account-node-1
Node-1 creates the namespace
Invite node-2 to the namespace
Node-2 joins the namespace
Node-1 creates the context
Node-2 enrolls a device for a fresh account
Read Alice's account off her laptop
Node-1 grants Alice's account as a writer
The granted writer set, as node-1 sees it
Alice's account is a writer
The grant landed on both nodes
The laptop writes the shared value
Node-1 reads the laptop's write
The granted device's write converged
Pair node-3 onto Alice's account
The pairing delivered a scope key and minted a credential
Read the account the phone speaks for
The phone speaks for the same account as the laptop
The phone writes the shared value
Node-1 reads the phone's write
Node-2 reads the phone's write
The writer set as node-1 sees it after the phone's write
An ungranted device of a granted account wrote, and converged
The laptop files an authored entry
The phone updates the laptop's authored entry
Node-1 reads the authored entry
The second device's update landed, and propagated
The two devices authored as one account but distinct replicas
